title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Service Discovery

objectives: Why is hardcoding IP addresses or DNS hostnames insufficient for a microservices system?
Contrast client-side and server-side discovery. When is each preferable?
Why does Netflix Eureka choose AP (availability + partition tolerance) over CP (consistency)?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Service discovery is the mechanism by which services in a microservices system locate each other at runtime — a registry tracks live instances, clients or proxies query it to find healthy endpoints, and instances register and deregister via heartbeats so the registry always reflects the current topology.

In a monolith, service-to-service calls are function pointers — the caller knows the callee's address at compile time because they share a process. In a microservices system, service instances come and go constantly: autoscaling adds pods, deploys replace instances, crashes remove them, and network partitions make some unreachable. Hardcoding IP addresses or hostnames breaks the moment any of these events occurs, which is every few minutes in a large cluster. Service discovery solves this by introducing a registry — a dynamic mapping from a logical service name (e.g., `billing-service`) to the set of currently-healthy network endpoints (IP:port pairs). Callers query the registry at call time (or cache its results with a short TTL), get back a list of live instances, and pick one — typically via client-side load balancing (round-robin, weighted, or latency-aware). Netflix built Eureka in 2012 precisely because their microservices fleet was too dynamic for DNS or a static config file; today Kubernetes Services + kube-dns and HashiCorp Consul are the dominant implementations, and service meshes like Istio and Linkerd layer their own discovery on top.

The two architectural patterns are **client-side discovery** and **server-side discovery**. In client-side discovery (Netflix Eureka + Ribbon), the client queries the registry directly, gets the full list of instances, and chooses one itself — this gives the client full control over load-balancing policy (weighted, latency-aware, zone-affinity) but couples every client to the registry's client library and means every language must implement the library. In server-side discovery (Kubernetes Services, AWS ALB, Envoy), the client calls a stable virtual address (a Service IP, an ALB DNS name) and a router in front of the instances picks one — this decouples clients from the registry but limits the load-balancing policy to whatever the router supports. The trade-off is flexibility vs simplicity: Netflix chose client-side because they wanted fine-grained control (zone-affinity, latency-aware routing, canary weights), while most Kubernetes users choose server-side because the kube-proxy + Service abstraction is built into the platform and works for any language. Hybrid patterns exist: a service mesh like Istio puts an Envoy sidecar next to every service, so the application makes a localhost call to Envoy, which does client-side discovery against the registry and applies sophisticated routing — the application sees server-side simplicity while the sidecar has client-side power.

The registry itself is a distributed system with its own consistency and availability trade-offs. Netflix Eureka is famously AP — it prioritizes availability over consistency, so during a network partition a registry node may serve stale instance lists (pointing to instances that are actually down) rather than refuse the query. This is the right trade-off for discovery because a stale answer that is then validated by a health check is better than no answer, and clients must already handle transient failures with retries and circuit breakers. Consul and etcd are CP — they use Raft consensus, so a partition makes the minority side refuse writes to preserve consistency, which is the right choice when the registry is also used for configuration or leadership election but adds latency to discovery. Kubernetes uses etcd (CP) as the backing store but serves discovery from a local cache in each kube-proxy, so the steady-state path is fast and only the rare update pays the consensus cost. The architect's rule: pick AP for pure discovery (Eureka, Consul in AP mode), pick CP when the registry coordinates writes (etcd for Kubernetes, ZooKeeper for Kafka).

Health checking is the other half of discovery — a registry that lists dead instances is worse than no registry, because callers waste time retrying unreachable endpoints. Every registry implements two complementary mechanisms. **Passive health checks** are heartbeats: each instance sends a heartbeat every N seconds (Eureka: 30s), and the registry evicts instances that miss M consecutive heartbeats (Eureka: 3, so 90s). **Active health checks** are polls: the registry periodically calls each instance's health endpoint (Consul: HTTP GET /health, Kubernetes: liveness/readiness probes) and marks instances unhealthy if the check fails. Both are needed because they catch different failures: heartbeats catch network partitions and process crashes, active checks catch the "zombie" state where the process is alive but cannot serve (e.g., deadlocked, out of memory, dependent DB is down). Kubernetes formalizes this as liveness vs readiness probes — liveness controls whether the pod is restarted, readiness controls whether traffic is routed to it — and a correctly-configured service has both, because routing traffic to a pod that is alive-but-not-ready is a common production bug. The combination of registry + health checks + client retries is what makes a microservices system resilient to the constant churn of instances.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S1 as Billing Instance 1
    participant S2 as Billing Instance 2
    participant R as Service Registry
    participant C as Caller (Orders)
    participant H as Health Checker

    S1->>R: register (host=10.0.1.5:8080)
    S2->>R: register (host=10.0.1.6:8080)
    loop every 30s
        S1->>R: heartbeat
        S2->>R: heartbeat
    end
    H->>S1: GET /health
    H->>R: mark S1 healthy
    C->>R: resolve "billing-service"
    R-->>C: [10.0.1.5:8080, 10.0.1.6:8080]
    C->>S1: POST /charge (picked client-side)
    S2--xR: missed 3 heartbeats
    R-->>C: next resolve returns only [10.0.1.5:8080]
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +-----------+      register       +---------------------+
   | Instance1 | ------------------> |                     |
   | 10.0.1.5  | ---heartbeat/30s--> |   Service Registry  |
   +-----------+                     |   (live endpoints)  |
                                     |                     |
   +-----------+      register       |  billing-service:   |
   | Instance2 | ------------------> |   [10.0.1.5,        |
   | 10.0.1.6  | ---heartbeat/30s--> |    10.0.1.6]        |
   +-----------+                     |                     |
        ^                            +----------+----------+
        |  GET /health                          |
        +------- active probe (Health Checker) |
                                              |
   +-----------+   resolve("billing-service")  |
   |  Caller   | <-----------------------------+
   |  (Orders) |   returns [10.0.1.5, 10.0.1.6]
   +-----+-----+
         | pick one (client-side LB), POST /charge
         v
   +-----------+
   | Instance1 |
   +-----------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. Each billing instance registers itself with the registry on startup (host:port, metadata, health endpoint) and sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds; the health checker also polls each instance's `/health` endpoint actively.
2. When the caller (Orders service) needs to call billing, it queries the registry for "billing-service" and receives the current list of healthy endpoints; client-side load balancing picks one (round-robin, latency-aware, or zone-affinity).
3. If Instance2 crashes or misses 3 heartbeats, the registry evicts it; the next resolve call returns only Instance1, so the caller stops sending traffic to the dead instance. The whole cycle — registration, heartbeat, eviction, re-resolution — happens in tens of seconds with no operator intervention.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Minimal service registry with heartbeat, active health check, and lookup.
# Demonstrates client-side discovery: callers query the registry, pick an instance.

import threading, time, random, uuid
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Instance:
    service: str
    host: str
    port: int
    last_heartbeat: float = field(default_factory=time.time)
    healthy: bool = True

class ServiceRegistry:
    HEARTBEAT_TTL = 60          # evict after 60s without heartbeat
    EVICT_INTERVAL = 10        # sweep every 10s

    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = threading.RLock()
        self._instances = defaultdict(dict)   # service -> {instance_id: Instance}
        threading.Thread(target=self._evict_loop, daemon=True).start()

    def register(self, service, host, port):
        iid = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]
        inst = Instance(service, host, port)
        with self._lock:
            self._instances[service][iid] = inst
        return iid

    def heartbeat(self, service, iid):
        with self._lock:
            inst = self._instances[service].get(iid)
            if inst:
                inst.last_heartbeat = time.time()

    def resolve(self, service):
        with self._lock:
            return [(i.host, i.port) for i in self._instances[service].values()
                    if i.healthy]

    def _evict_loop(self):
        while True:
            now = time.time()
            with self._lock:
                for service, insts in self._instances.items():
                    dead = [iid for iid, i in insts.items()
                            if now - i.last_heartbeat > self.HEARTBEAT_TTL]
                    for iid in dead:
                        print(f"[registry] evicting {service}/{iid} (heartbeat lost)")
                        del insts[iid]
            time.sleep(self.EVICT_INTERVAL)

# --- Simulate: 2 instances register, one stops heartbeating, caller resolves ---
reg = ServiceRegistry()
iid1 = reg.register("billing", "10.0.1.5", 8080)
iid2 = reg.register("billing", "10.0.1.6", 8080)
print("Initial resolve:", reg.resolve("billing"))

# Instance 2 stops heartbeating (simulated crash)
time.sleep(2)
reg.heartbeat("billing", iid1)        # only 1 keeps heartbeating

# Force an eviction sweep by waiting past TTL scaled down (here, immediate check)
for _ in range(10):
    reg.heartbeat("billing", iid1)
    time.sleep(0.5)

print("After crash resolve:", reg.resolve("billing"))
```

options: Autoscaling and rolling deploys are the events that make discovery necessary, and the registry must keep up with them in real time.

quiz.explanation: Kubernetes provides discovery through three layers that compose cleanly. First, every Service has a stable virtual IP (the ClusterIP) that does not change for the Service's lifetime, and a stable DNS name (billing-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local) that resolves to that IP via kube-dns (CoreDNS in modern clusters).
